{"task": {"id": "I_kwDOVQjccM8AAAABbHmA8g", "item_id": "PVTI_lAHOAHSLSM4Bn3IfzhEstzM", "project_id": "PVT_kwHOAHSLSM4Bn3If", "number": 91, "title": "Complete internal EEPROM erase and bulk-command handling with hardware-grounded semantics", "body": "## Problem

The emulator now implements the console's **internal EEPROM** (Mono 128 B; WonderSwan Color and SwanCrystal 2048 B each), but `crates/ws-core/src/internal_eeprom.rs` explicitly rejects the remaining erase/bulk command families:

- **ERASE** (opcode 3, single-word erase via control bit `0x40`);
- **WRAL** (opcode 0, subcommand 1, write-all using the data latch);
- **ERAL** (opcode 0, subcommand 2, erase-all).

The current controller only accepts READ, WRITE, EWEN and EWDS; consequently programs that exercise additional supported commands fail with `Unsupported internal EEPROM command ...`. The **cartridge** EEPROM already implements these families, but the console EEPROM has distinct registers, protection, address modes and status behavior. It would be incorrect to copy cartridge semantics indiscriminately.

**Evidence caveat:** The public [ws-test-suite internal EEPROM experiment](https://github.com/asiekierka/ws-test-suite/blob/7dfa0e2e869d08386b685d6a56df0bcfaf181b47/src/mono/eeprom/internal/main.c) explicitly comments that direct ERASE seems unable to erase words other than word zero and substitutes WRITE `0xFFFF`. This is a *question*, not a proven silicon rule. Do not claim universal direct ERASE or destructive bulk operations work on physical consoles without evidence. Establish and document the most defensible behavior before finalizing acceptance expectations.

This milestone should close a **clearly identified missing hardware interface**, without requiring retail ROMs, proprietary firmware, physical-device access or the reuse of other emulator implementations.

## Expected outcome

- Internal EEPROM commands covered by verified public hardware definitions or sufficiently corroborated independent evidence execute through the existing **BA–BF / BE** register interface with correct command decoding, address-mode behavior, write enable/lock, settings protection, status and bounded shared-clock progression.
- Implement a hardware-grounded single-word ERASE path and **resolve WRAL/ERAL** against independent primary definitions/tests. Where a command's physical behavior is supported, implement it with real byte mutations. Where the internal controller's support or effects are genuinely unconfirmed/unsupported, retain a specific diagnostic and document the evidence gap instead of inventing a full-memory erase.
- Preserve the model-specific console records, ROM/cartridge save isolation, existing ordinary EEPROM transfers, and native/Wasm/browser persistence.
- Verify using original **CC0** source-included machine-code fixtures and deterministic Rust/browser tests, not commercial games.

## Context and reproduction

Inspect the current `main` before editing:

- [`crates/ws-core/src/internal_eeprom.rs`](https://github.com/takahirox/wonderswan-rust/blob/main/crates/ws-core/src/internal_eeprom.rs) contains `Operation::{Read, Write, Enable, Locked}` but no erase/bulk cases. The `write(0xBE, ...)` match rejects other opcode/subcommand/control combinations, and `tick()` applies only ordinary operations. Existing `handoff`/sticky protection must survive.
- [`crates/ws-core/src/internal_eeprom_tests.rs`](https://github.com/takahirox/wonderswan-rust/blob/main/crates/ws-core/src/internal_eeprom_tests.rs) explicitly tests that unsupported erase/bulk commands do not mutate data; update relevant tests to distinguish supported operations from truly unsupported/malformed combinations.
- [`crates/ws-core/src/eeprom.rs`](https://github.com/takahirox/wonderswan-rust/blob/main/crates/ws-core/src/eeprom.rs) implements **cartridge** ERASE/WRAL/ERAL, but its C4–C9 interface, mapper-specific DONE quirk, behavior on bit 7 and absence of console-settings protection are different. Reference conceptually only; do not merge controllers or port behavior without independent evidence.
- [`docs/hardware-subset.md`](https://github.com/takahirox/wonderswan-rust/blob/main/docs/hardware-subset.md#internal-eeprom-transfers-retention-and-api) documents internal READ/WRITE, six/ten address-bit modes, BE READY/DONE, 0x60-protected settings boundary, approximate latencies, and persisted records for three physical models. Issue [#21](https://github.com/takahirox/wonderswan-rust/issues/21) established these invariants.
- [`fixtures/`](https://github.com/takahirox/wonderswan-rust/tree/main/fixtures) contains original source/reproducible CC0 probes; [`web/scripts/compat.mjs`](https://github.com/takahirox/wonderswan-rust/blob/main/web/scripts/compat.mjs) tests the real Wasm player, local storage and reload.

### Independent references and uncertainty

Use these **hardware definitions and original experiments**, not another emulator's implementation:

1. [Wonderful Toolchain hardware definitions: internal EEPROM registers](https://github.com/WonderfulToolchain/hardware-definitions/blob/main/target/wswan/eeprom.xml): BA data, BC command, BE `ERASE` (bit 6), WRITE (bit 5), READ (bit 4), PROTECT (bit 7), READY and DONE.
2. [libws erase-word assembly](https://github.com/WonderfulToolchain/target-wswan-syslibs/blob/main/libws/src/eeprom/eeprom_erase_word.s) sends an ERASE opcode and `0x40` control. This establishes a documented software sequence, **not proof that every internal word is erasable**.
3. [ws-test-suite internal EEPROM experiment](https://github.com/asiekierka/ws-test-suite/blob/7dfa0e2e869d08386b685d6a56df0bcfaf181b47/src/mono/eeprom/internal/main.c): it avoids direct erase on internal EEPROM due to the explicitly stated uncertainty, substitutes writing `0xFFFF`, and does not certify WRAL/ERAL support.
4. [WSdev: Internal EEPROM](https://ws.nesdev.org/wiki/Internal_EEPROM), [libws EEPROM API and protection](https://github.com/WonderfulToolchain/target-wswan-syslibs/blob/main/libws/include/ws/eeprom.h) and [console I/O register descriptions](https://wonderful.asie.pl/doc/libws/ports_8h_source.html).

Before implementing a destructive command, write a brief **source reconciliation** distinguishing *confirmed hardware facts*, *plausible implementation policies* and *unverified behavior*. A generic 93Cx6 Microwire instruction table or cartridge EEPROM implementation by itself is **not evidence** that the same bulk command is supported by the console interface. Do not overstate the outcome.

## Implementation requirements

### A. Command decoding and state

1. Extend the existing internal controller's command decode for the **evidence-supported subset** of ERASE/WRAL/ERAL, with source-based opcode/subcommand, start bit, command width and BE control-bit rules. Keep malformed formats, multiple control bits, busy-controller requests and genuinely unsupported commands visibly rejected without altering completed storage.
2. Support Mono 6-bit word addresses and active Color 10-bit word addresses, including Color/Crystal switching into/out of mono graphics mode. The **physical** EEPROM size is always determined by console model; changing graphics mode must neither erase nor resize data. Byte/word IN/OUT to BA–BF must retain their established semantics.
3. Snapshot command parameters (selected address/data, applicable write-enable state) when a command is accepted. Preserve the existing separate read and write data buffers, reserved `0xBF` behavior, and command readback. Changes to BA/BC, video mode, subsequent control writes or model lifecycle must not reinterpret in-flight requests.
4. Preserve the existing BE bit 7 *sticky settings protection* and the independent WEN/WDS write lock. Neither a single ERASE nor a bulk operation may circumvent protection of offsets `0x60` and above. Distinguish initial authorization from protection at completion, consistent with existing WRITE semantics. In particular, test the 0x5E/0x60 boundary and the 128/2048-byte final words.
5. If a bulk operation is independently evidenced, specify whether it affects all bytes, only the writable user area, or is limited by settings protection, and implement that exact policy. If no reliable internal-controller semantics can be established, do **not** invent blanket erasure; document the command as unresolved with precise, specific errors and evidence, and make explicit why it remains unsupported.

### B. Timing, lifecycle and safety

1. Use the current deterministic shared-clock/pending-operation model for supported commands. The existing 32-clock READ and 3072-clock WRITE/WEN/WDS intervals are *approximations*, not measured EEPROM erase latencies; select and explain a bounded ERASE/bulk latency policy from the best available evidence rather than claiming exact timing.
2. READY/BUSY transitions and DONE/read buffer behavior must be explicit and independently tested for command start, pending progress and completion. No operation should block the browser event loop or perform unbounded per-cycle work.
3. A pending command is discarded on reset/ROM replace/model switch as established by Issue #21; completed writes/erases survive permitted lifecycle changes and browser reload. Invalid ROM loads, failed imports and incompatible model transitions must preserve established EEPROM records.
4. Prevent accidental out-of-bounds access, partial unintended bulk erasure, corruption of another model's console data or a cartridge SRAM/external EEPROM save. Do not introduce implicit wipe-on-boot, wipe-on-unknown-command or a new destructive UI control.

### C. Original test coverage and documentation

1. Extend the Rust unit tests and add a **source-included CC0 V30MZ homebrew probe** (or extend the existing internal EEPROM probe) that executes real OUT/IN instruction sequences for the supported ERASE and any evidenced bulk commands, polls BE status and verifies full data and/or selected markers. The fixture must not rely on existing commercial ROMs or proprietary BIOS. Fixtures must not depend on a physical console.
2. Cover both console modes and all three physical models, ordinary READ/WRITE/WEN/WDS regressions, protection/lock transitions, busy rejection and invalid combinations; test storage before and after command completion, async reset while pending, and boundary words.
3. Verify native storage contents and the **real Wasm browser path**, including per-model records, a different cartridge, page reload/reopen, and corrupt/denied/full browser storage. Existing original gameplay, audio, GDMA/SDMA, RTC, video and cartridge save tests must keep working.
4. Update `docs/hardware-subset.md`, any fixture provenance and user docs where relevant; explicitly label resolved behavior vs conjectural/synthetic timing. Keep one focused Issue; do not build a new generic tracing framework or unrelated settings UI.

## Pre-merge acceptance criteria

- [ ] A short review of independent **primary hardware definitions + available experiment evidence** establishes the supported ERASE and any supported bulk command semantics, and explicitly records uncertainties (notably the observed/questioned direct-ERASE word-zero restriction). **Do not derive internal EEPROM bulk support solely from cartridge EEPROM behavior.**
- [ ] Implement and test the defensible internal ERASE path with correct command format, controller status and actual data changes for the corroborated address cases; any unresolved cases have precise non-destructive handling. For WRAL/ERAL, implement genuine effects only when evidence is adequate; otherwise retain explicit, documented rejection rather than falsely claiming support. Explain the resolution for **each** operation.
- [ ] Tests cover every supported command on Mono, Color and Crystal; six/ten-bit command widths, active color/mono modes, edge addresses, address/data capture, write-lock and sticky settings protection, data-buffer separation, in-flight requests and status changes.
- [ ] Native tests verify timing progression and bounded completion for supported operations during scanlines/timers/audio/GDMA/SDMA, without creating a second clock or regressing current READ/WRITE behavior.
- [ ] A reproducible, original **CC0 CPU-executed cartridge test** covers supported new commands and meaningful locked/protected/busy/invalid edge cases. Its source and expected observations are included, with no proprietary ROM/BIOS or other emulator code.
- [ ] Rust core, WebAssembly and production-preview Chromium tests verify the resulting console bytes and cross-cartridge/model/browser persistence, including safety on failures. Existing save, sound, video, playable demo and other compatibility probes still pass.
- [ ] The normal mandatory commands pass and actual results are documented: `python3 fixtures/build.py --check`, `python3 demo/build.py --check`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo test --workspace --locked`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings`, `git diff --check`, and in `web`: `npm ci`, `npm run build:wasm`, `npm run build`, `npm run test:browser`, `npm run test:compat`.
- [ ] All exposed ports retain correct model gating and reserved-bit behavior; existing ROM/save bytes and web UI are not modified for unrelated reasons. Update support documentation to reflect exactly what was implemented or left unresolved.

## Optional validation

Independent physical-console test measurements of ERASE/WRAL/ERAL on **non-sensitive user-area words only**, or additional permissively licensed verified hardware vectors. Physical testing must not accidentally erase device owner/settings information, and is optional—not a prerequisite. Never require commercial ROMs or real-user EEPROM dumps.

## Required post-merge verification

1. **Pending:** Confirm the `main` GitHub Pages deployment workflow succeeds for the merge commit and record the Actions run and revision.
2. **Pending:** Load the original source-included EEPROM probe on the public player and verify the supported new operation(s), status, model isolation and persistence through reload, distinguishing tested browser behavior from physical hardware fidelity.

These deployment-only checks are not pre-merge acceptance gates.
